lesson.title: defaultdict: Missing Keys That Fix Themselves
lesson.summary: collections.defaultdict automatically creates a default value the first time a missing key is accessed, using a factory function you supply, which removes the need for manual key-existence checks scattered through your code.
lesson.body:
You have already seen the idea of a default value before, whether as a function parameter that falls back to some sensible value when the caller does not supply one, or as dict.get(key, default), which returns a fallback instead of raising an error when a key is missing. defaultdict, from the same collections module that gave you namedtuple and OrderedDict, takes that idea and bakes it directly into the dictionary itself, so every single lookup benefits from it automatically, not just the ones where you remembered to call .get().

A plain dict raises a KeyError the instant you try to access a key that is not there. That forces a familiar and slightly clunky pattern: check whether the key exists first, and if it does not, create it with some starting value before you can update it. defaultdict removes that ceremony. You construct it by passing a factory function, a callable with no arguments that produces the default, most commonly list, int, or set. The first time you access a key that is not yet present, defaultdict calls that factory, stores the result under that key, and gives it back to you, all without raising an error.

```python
from collections import defaultdict

word_lengths = defaultdict(list)
words = ["cat", "dog", "ant", "owl", "cow", "pig"]

for word in words:
    word_lengths[len(word)].append(word)

print(dict(word_lengths))

counts = defaultdict(int)
for word in words:
    counts[word[0]] += 1

print(dict(counts))
```

In the first loop, word_lengths[len(word)] is accessed for a key that starts out missing every time a new word length shows up. Instead of crashing, defaultdict(list) calls list() to produce an empty list, stores it under that key, and then .append(word) works immediately on that fresh empty list. Every word here has length 3, so all six end up grouped under a single key. In the second loop, counts[word[0]] += 1 relies on defaultdict(int) supplying 0 the first time each starting letter appears, so += 1 always has a number to add to, never a missing key. The output is:

```
{3: ['cat', 'dog', 'ant', 'owl', 'cow', 'pig']}
{'c': 2, 'd': 1, 'a': 1, 'o': 1, 'p': 1}
```

Notice that 'c' ends with a count of 2, because both "cat" and "cow" start with c, and every other letter that appears exactly once shows a count of 1. Without defaultdict, that counting loop would need an explicit check along the lines of if word[0] not in counts: counts[word[0]] = 0 before the increment could safely run. defaultdict folds that check into the container itself, which is why it shows up constantly in code that groups or tallies things.
